title: Have all the good ideas already been discovered?
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant examine whether all the good ideas have already been discovered. They open with the show's milestone count and a study on early humans attaching handles to stone tools, then discuss the claim (attributed to Patent Office commissioner Charles Duell) that everything has been invented, and economists Cedric Lagarde and Eric Verdier's view that smartphones repackage existing technology and that innovation is stalled by short tech refresh cycles. They discuss Edmund Phelps's argument that money and government subsidies matter for innovation, and the NIH Director's New Innovator Award winners (Dino Di Carlo, Hu Wang, Jin Young Lee) working on nanoparticle cell control, graphene cancer detection, and optogenetic fMRI. The episode then turns to limits of discovery: Russell Stannard's The End of Discovery, Kant's noumenon, subjectivism and solipsism, quantum observation, Hawking and Mlodinow's The Grand Design and the theory of everything, and Ramachandran's five revolutions. A listener mail from Peyton about autocorrect closes the show.
topics: have all good ideas been discovered
Russell Stannard The End of Discovery

segments.title: Opening banter and early stone tools
segments.summary: Hosts note the show's roughly 300th episode milestone, then discuss a study on why early humans took about two million years to attach handles to sharp stone tools, linked to a brain region in the right hemisphere.

segments.title: Has everything been invented?
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the rapid pace of innovation since the Industrial Revolution and the attributed quote by Patent Office commissioner Charles Duell that everything has been invented. They argue that claiming innovation has plateaued shows a lack of historical awareness.

segments.title: Stalled tech innovation and repackaging
segments.summary: Lagarde and Verdier argue that smartphones repackage existing technologies and that hardware innovation has become design-driven. The hosts summarize their predictions of hardware consolidation and green-driven innovation, and their point that short tech refresh cycles reduce investment.

segments.title: Money, subsidies and garage innovators
segments.summary: Edmund Phelps argues that too little money goes to innovation and that government subsidies flow mainly to big business. The hosts disagree, saying garage innovators act from the urge to make ideas real rather than for money, and they discuss a proposed national innovation bank and NIH grants.

segments.title: NIH New Innovator Award winners
segments.summary: The hosts profile three UCLA researchers who won the NIH Director's New Innovator Award. Dino Di Carlo uses magnets and nanoparticles to apply heat, pressure or chemicals to specific cell sites; Hu Wang uses graphene sensors to detect cancer early; Jin Young Lee combines optogenetics with fMRI to study specific neurons.

segments.title: Limits of discovery and subjectivity
segments.summary: The hosts debate whether major discoveries remain, citing Russell Stannard's The End of Discovery and the idea that human brains may have limits. They discuss Kant's noumenon, subjectivism, solipsism, and quantum observation as reasons some aspects of reality may remain unknowable.

segments.title: Theory of everything and scientific revolutions
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Hawking and Mlodinow's The Grand Design, which suggests a family of interconnected theories rather than a single theory of everything. They also cover Ramachandran's five revolutions and whether consensus reflects reality accurately.

segments.title: Wrap-up and closing
segments.summary: Hosts summarize that they are not out of new ideas and point listeners to related articles on the site about innovation, discovery and neurons.

segments.title: Listener mail: Peyton and autocorrect
segments.summary: Listener Peyton, age thirteen, shares a mock idea for a website collecting funny iPhone autocorrect mistakes. The hosts close with a request for overlooked movie suggestions and the show's sign-off.
